question: A breastfeeding woman with confirmed lactational breast abscess (3 cm diameter, fluctuant, ultrasound-confirmed unilocular) is being managed. Which is the preferred first-line drainage approach according to current evidence?

answers.text: Open incision and drainage under general anaesthesia in the operating theatre

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Open I&D under GA was the traditional approach but is now second-line for unilocular abscesses — it requires a hospital stay, a longer healing wound, and stops breastfeeding more reliably than aspiration.

Correct. Ultrasound-guided aspiration (repeated at 2–3-day intervals if reaccumulation occurs) with concurrent antibiotics is the current preferred first-line approach for unilocular abscesses ≤5 cm. It is as effective as I&D, preserves breastfeeding, avoids GA, and leaves a better cosmetic result.

answers.text: Antibiotics alone with close monitoring, as the abscess may resolve without drainage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A confirmed abscess requires drainage — antibiotics alone are insufficient once pus has formed, as the avascular cavity is not penetrated by antibiotics effectively.
Mastectomy is not indicated for a lactational breast abscess. This is an extreme and inappropriate intervention for a condition that responds well to aspiration and antibiotics.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: once fluctuance/pus is confirmed, drainage is mandatory. Ultrasound-guided aspiration is now preferred over traditional open I&D for unilocular abscesses.
Well done. Ultrasound-guided aspiration is preferred for small unilocular abscesses — it preserves breastfeeding and has equivalent cure rates to surgical I&D.
